etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English damage, from Old French damage, from Vulgar Latin *damnāticum from Classical Latin damnum. Compare modern French dommage. Displaced Middle English scath.

definitions.definition: Injury or harm; the condition or measure of something not being intact.

quote.citation: 1625, Francis [Bacon], “Of Friendship”, in The Essayes […], 3rd edition, London:  […]  Iohn Haviland for Hanna Barret, →OCLC:
quote.text: Great errors and absurdities many  […] commit for want of a friend to tell them of them, to the great damage both of their fame and fortune.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To impair the soundness, goodness, or value of; to harm or cause destruction.

quote.citation: 1774, Edward Long, The History of Jamaica. Or, General Survey of the Antient and Modern State of that Island, volume 2, book 2, chapter 7, 5:
quote.text: The building was erected in two years, at the parochial expence, on the foundation of the former one, which was irreparably damaged by the hurricane of Auguſt, 1712.

quote.citation: 1702–1704, Edward [Hyde, 1st] Earl of Clarendon, “(please specify |book=I to XVI)”, in The History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England, Begun in the Year 1641. […], Oxford, Oxfordshire: Printed at the Theater, published 1707, →OCLC:
quote.text: He  […]  came up to the English admiral and gave him a broadside, with which he killed many of his men and damaged the ship.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, obsolete) To undergo damage; to take damage.
(transitive) To remove a damaged or unsalable item from the sales floor for processing.
